Content:
Adding a value to [MATH: y=2^x] will translate (shift) the exponential function up or down the [MATH: y]-axis.

Content:
For instance, adding [MATH: 3] to [MATH: y=2^x] will move each point on the exponential function [MATH: 3] units up.

Note the following points:

Content:
1. The [MATH: y]-intercept [MATH: (0,1)] has moved up [MATH: 3] units to the point [MATH: (0,4).]

items.title: Combining Vertical Shift and Vertical Stretch

sections.normalized_html: When an exponential growth function is vertically shifted and stretched, we apply the stretch first and the shift second.
sections.readable_text: When an exponential growth function is vertically shifted and stretched, we apply the stretch first and the shift second.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The horizontal asymptote of the curve [MATH: y=k(6^{x})+c] is [MATH: y=c.] In the graph above, the horizontal asymptote is [MATH: y=4], so [MATH: c=4.]

Therefore, our function takes the form

[MATH: y=k(6^{x})+4.]

We can solve for [MATH: k] by finding a point on the graph and substituting for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] The labeled point on the graph is [MATH: (0,6),] so we substitute [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: y=6] into the function and solve for [MATH: k\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: y|= k(6^{x}) + 4; 6|= k(6^{0}) + 4; 6|= k(1) + 4; 6|= k + 4; 2|= k]

Therefore, the curve is [MATH: y=2(6^{x})+4.]

Therefore, our function takes the form

We can solve for [MATH: k] by finding a point on the graph and substituting for [MATH: x] and [MATH: y.] The labeled point on the graph is [MATH: (0,6),] so we substitute [MATH: x=0] and [MATH: y=6] into the function and solve for [MATH: k\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: y|= k(6^{x}) + 4; 6|= k(6^{0}) + 4; 6|= k(1) + 4; 6|= k + 4; 2|= k]

Therefore, the curve is [MATH: y=2(6^{x})+4.]
